\section[bonum vesperum]{bonum vesperum — the accusative rule returns, this time visibly}

\label{lesson:LA-C34-bonum-vesperum}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Two lessons ago, \emph{bonum māne} couldn't show you Latin's real wish-grammar, because \emph{māne} is neuter. This time it's back — because \emph{vesper} isn't.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: bonum vesperum — masculine, and the case shows again}]
\textbf{Bonum vesperum} = "\textbf{good evening}." Like \emph{bonam noctem} and \emph{bonum māne}, this specific phrase is \textbf{not} classically attested as a fixed Roman greeting — the same honest gap, a third time. But the grammar here is different from \emph{bonum māne}'s: \textbf{vesper} is \textbf{masculine}, and Latin masculine nouns genuinely \textbf{do} distinguish nominative (\emph{vesper}) from accusative (\emph{vesperum}) — unlike neuter \emph{māne}, where the two forms were always identical. So \emph{bonum vesperum} \textbf{does} demonstrate the real Accusative-of-Exclamation rule again, the same wish-construction behind \emph{bonam noctem} and the genuinely attested \emph{Fēlīcem nātālem!} — just dressed in masculine endings instead of feminine ones.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: A feminine alternate: bonam vesperam}]
Latin also has a separate \textbf{feminine} noun for evening, \textbf{vespera} (distinct from masculine \emph{vesper}, though built from the same root — both headwords appeared together last lesson, though without their genders spelled out). Paired with \emph{bonus}, its accusative gives \textbf{bonam vesperam} — agreeing the \textbf{same way} \emph{bonam noctem} does: the adjective, \emph{bonam}, matches \emph{bonam} exactly. But watch the \textbf{nouns} carefully — they do \textbf{not} share an ending. \emph{Vespera} is \textbf{1st declension} (accusative \emph{-am}, \emph{vesperam}), while \emph{nox} is \textbf{3rd declension} (accusative \emph{-em}, \emph{noctem} — \textbf{not} \emph{-am}). Same adjective agreement, genuinely different noun declensions underneath.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} Is \emph{bonum vesperum} itself directly attested as a classical Roman greeting? (\textbf{No} — a modern, pedagogical phrase, like \emph{bonam noctem} and \emph{bonum māne}.) Why does \emph{bonum vesperum} show the real Accusative-of-Exclamation rule, when \emph{bonum māne} couldn't? (\textbf{Vesper is masculine}, and masculine nouns distinguish nominative from accusative; \emph{māne} is neuter, where the two are always identical.) What's the feminine alternate, and how does its adjective agreement compare to \emph{bonam noctem}'s? (\textbf{Bonam vesperam} — the adjective \emph{bonam} matches \emph{bonam} exactly, but the NOUNS don't share an ending: \emph{vesperam} is 1st declension \emph{-am}, while \emph{noctem} is 3rd declension \emph{-em}, not \emph{-am}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
